articles_hidden.title: Functional redundancy between atypical CDKs reveals a vulnerability in hepatocellular carcinoma
articles_hidden.authors: Diego Martínez-Alonso, Enrique Nogueira, Luis R. López-Sainz, Alexis P. Pérez, Carolina Villarroya-Beltri, Alejandro Garcia-Diaz, Gloria C. Bonel-Pérez, Aicha El Bakkali, Senn Wakahashi, Agustín Sánchez-Belmonte, Isabel García-Cao, Jesus Castillo-Sanchez, José González-Martínez, Diego Megias, Jana Sánchez, Stephan Geley, Javier Muñoz, Sagrario Ortega, Fleur M. Ferguson, Nathanael S. Gray, David J. Shields, Amaia Lujambio, Guillermo de Cárcer, Marcos Malumbres
articles_hidden.abstract: The atypical cyclin-dependent kinase subfamily (CDK14–18) encompasses five related proteins with unclear function, and for which individual depletion has not demonstrated sustained therapeutic relevance. We report here that CDK16 and CDK18 compensate each other and liver cancer cells are sensitive to the concomitant inactivation of both kinases, resulting in persistent defects in DNA repair and subsequent cell death. These effects are linked to a role of CDK16/18 in regulating nucleocytoplasmatic transport through phosphorylation of nuclear pore complex components, including NUP35. Genetic ablation of Cdk16 and Cdk18 in established liver tumors driven by MYC and beta-catenin oncogenes triggers DNA damage in cancer cells without affecting adjacent normal tissue, ultimately leading to tumor regression. Collectively, these findings provide a rationale for the development of CDK16–18 inhibitors—likely targeting multiple subfamily members due to their structural similarity—as a strategy against aggressive cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, where effective treatment options remain limited.

articles_hidden.title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Guénon, Marion Chauveau, Karolina Filipowska, Iñaki Tuñón, Clément Nizak, Kimberly A. Reynolds, Guillaume Stirnemann, Olivier Rivoire, Damien Laage
articles_hidden.abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

articles_hidden.title: A voltage-gated porin PPE1 regulates secretion and drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
articles_hidden.authors: Mohit Yadav, Neilah Firzan C. A., Dipanwita Mandal, Jyotsna Shukla, Binayak Sarkar, Sanjeet Kumar Mahtha, Aakash Chandramouli, Abhishek Prasad, Siddhesh S. Kamat, Debasisa Mohanty, Somnath Dutta, Kozhinjampara R. Mahendran, Rajesh S. Gokhale
articles_hidden.abstract: Drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) remains a formidable clinical hurdle, compounded by the fact that the pathways by which antibiotics penetrate its multilayered cell envelope remain incompletely mapped. We identify PPE1 as a voltage-gated outer-membrane porin that mediates the secretion of kupyaphores while also facilitating the uptake of the frontline anti-tubercular drug isoniazid (INH). Genome-wide association analysis of 38,038 clinical isolates links ppe1 mutations with INH resistance, highlighting its clinical relevance. Consistent with this, the Mtb Δ ppe1 mutant shows increased tolerance to INH, accompanied by markedly reduced intracellular accumulation of INH compared with the wild-type strain. The Δ ppe1 strain exhibits attenuated infection, impaired growth, and reduced virulence in a murine infection model. Electron microscopy, molecular modeling, and single-channel electrophysiology reveal that PPE1 assembles into an unusual pentameric α-helical channel, distinct from classical β-barrel bacterial porins. Together, our findings identify PPE1 as a key determinant of mycobacterial membrane permeability that coordinates metallophore secretion and also antibiotic influx. This work uncovers a previously unrecognized mechanism governing Mtb physiology, virulence, and drug susceptibility, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

articles_hidden.title: A glycan superbinder reveals polysialylated-CD56 as a precision biomarker for pancreatic cancer
articles_hidden.authors: Lingrui Huang, Song Gao, Qi Li, Fang Jin, Anqi Zhang, Xiawen Lin, Yanrong Wen, Wenyan Guan, Jie Shen, Jian He, Zhen Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most lethal malignancies, largely due to the lack of reliable biomarkers for early detection. Aberrant glycosylation presents a promising source of diagnostic signatures, yet polysialic acid (polySia), a distinctive glycan, has remained underexplored, primarily owing to limitations in detection methods and recognition tools. Here, we report the development of a polySia “superbinder,” a nanoscale molecularly imprinted polymer (nanoMIP) that exhibits superior specificity and affinity for polySia over monoclonal antibodies, enabling precise recognition and quantification of this glycan. Leveraging this superbinder, we uncover a previously unrecognized association between polySia and pancreatic cancer and establish polysialylated CD56 (polySia-CD56) as a specific and robust biomarker. PolySia-CD56 outperforms multiple previously reported pancreatic cancer biomarkers, including the clinical standard carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9). Notably, its expression pattern is complementary to that of CA19-9, and the combined use of both biomarkers significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy to 94.1%, effectively addressing the limitation of CA19-9 in detecting CA19-9-negative patients. Together, this study not only identifies polySia-CD56 as a precise biomarker for pancreatic cancer but also highlights the potential of antiglycan nanoMIPs as transformative reagents for decoding glycosylated targets and advancing clinical translation.

articles_hidden.title: Rembrandt through the eyes of the machine: Toward explainable Human–AI collaboration in painting attribution
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Arias-Rosales, Arthur K. Wheelock, J. Kenneth Moritz, Philip R. LeDuc, Jonathan Cagan
articles_hidden.abstract: With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

articles_hidden.title: FMRI-guided focal transcranial magnetic stimulation of anterior cingulate cortex reduces opioid seeking and restores connectivity
articles_hidden.authors: Zilu Ma, Ying Duan, Hieu Nguyen, Sabrina Lin, Md Mohaiminul Haque, Danni Wang, Samantha Hoffman, Aidan Carney, Taylor Scott, Eleni Varlas, Elliot Stein, Zheng-Xiong Xi, Yavin Shaham, Hanbing Lu, Yihong Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Relapse remains a major challenge in opioid addiction treatment. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy for addiction, yet results had been mixed due to empirically selected stimulation targets and limited knowledge of neural circuit engagement. Here, we used a focal rat TMS platform to test whether high-density theta-burst stimulation (hdTBS) of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a corticostriatal node implicated in opioid relapse by prior causal and longitudinal functional MRI studies, decreases relapse-like oxycodone seeking and associated circuit dysfunction. Male rats self-administered oxycodone intravenously for 14 d and then underwent 13 d of electric barrier-induced abstinence, a procedure that suppresses drug taking while preserving drug availability and drug-associated context. During abstinence, the rats received seven daily sessions of sham stimulation or ACC-targeted hdTBS, with relapse tests and longitudinal functional MRI acquired during early and late abstinence to assess the behavioral and circuit-level effects of stimulation. Sham-treated rats showed a time-dependent increase (incubation) in oxycodone seeking and reduced ACC connectivity with dorsal and ventral striatum. In contrast, ACC-targeted hdTBS prevented incubation of oxycodone seeking and reversed abstinence-associated ACC-striatal connectivity reductions. Stimulation-sensitive functional circuits showed spatial correspondence with tracer-defined ACC projection patterns, suggesting that anatomical connectivity is critical to the circuit-level effects of focal stimulation. These findings support ACC-centered corticostriatal circuits as mechanistically informed targets for neuromodulation in opioid addiction and introduce a preclinical framework for linking stimulation, behavior, and longitudinal circuit remodeling.

articles_hidden.title: Ionic liquid–mediated cellular loading for whole tumor cell vaccines
articles_hidden.authors: Danika Rodrigues, Malini Mukherji, Kyung Soo Park, Maithili Joshi, Litsa Kapsalis, Suyog Shaha, Michael Griffith Bibbey, Metecan Erdi, Samir Mitragotri
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional whole tumor cell cancer vaccines have demonstrated limited clinical success due to insufficient immunogenicity and challenges in adjuvant codelivery, despite their rich antigen repertoire and high patient-specific activity. Here, we introduce a simple, single-step approach to load immunostimulatory CpG oligodeoxynucleotides into tumor cells undergoing immunogenic cell death using an ionic liquid–containing cocktail. Results indicate that these adjuvant-loaded tumor cells (referred to as IL-Vax) enhance the uptake of cell-based vaccines by dendritic cells and their subsequent activation, leading to potent antitumor immunity. IL-Vax offered strong protection against tumor growth in a prophylactic B16F10 melanoma mouse model. Furthermore, IL-Vax synergized with PD-1 blockade to slow tumor growth and extend survival in a therapeutic model. The modularity of IL-Vax enables the loading of different cargos or cargo combinations, which may be conducive for additional tailoring of such vaccines and potentially other cell loading applications.

articles_hidden.title: Capture and reduction of singlet oxygen via an anthracene-based framework for stable Li-O 2 batteries
articles_hidden.authors: Zhuoliang Jiang, Zhao Zhao, Liang Gao, Yifei Ma, Ke Liu, Jiaxuan An, Yaohui Huang, Zikang Chen, Xinlong Tian, Fujun Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Given the increasing global energy demand and rapid advancement of low-carbon technologies, Li-O 2 batteries have attracted considerable attention owing to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density, offering great promise for advanced energy systems. However, the formation of harmful singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ) in both discharge and charge processes induces parasitic reactions that deteriorate round-trip efficiency and cycling stability. Herein, an anthracene-based covalent-organic framework (AntCOF) is introduced as a highly effective catalyst for the 1 O 2 reduction reaction (SORR) in Li-O 2 batteries. The conjugated porous framework selectively captures electrophilic 1 O 2 , enabling effective charge transfer from AntCOF to the empty π* orbital of 1 O 2 and promoting SORR in subsequent discharge processes. This mechanism suppresses 1 O 2 diffusion and mitigates associated side reactions, leading to reduced overpotentials and improved cycling performance when coupled with a RuO 2 catalyst. This work may enlighten further investigations into 1 O 2 -related chemistry across a broad range of oxygen-redox electrochemical systems.

articles_hidden.title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Lingfeng Li, Zhuoyuan Li, Shun Li, Kaixin Zhan, Huajian Gao, Chang Qing Chen, Liu Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

articles_hidden.title: SMYD3-catalyzed dimethylation of gasdermin D at lysine 43 promotes pyroptosis and inflammatory responses
articles_hidden.authors: Zixuan Wang, Shuke Jia, Yiman Luo, Wen Liu, Xiaoli Zeng, Yuhan Xiang, Lele Yu, Hongyan Deng, Xueyi Sun, Chunchun Zhu, Wuhan Xiao, Xing Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Gasdermin D (GSDMD), a key pyroptosis effector downstream of inflammasome activation, undergoes precise regulation by multiple posttranslational modifications. Here, we identify SMYD3, a lysine methyltransferase, as a positive regulator of GSDMD. SMYD3 interacts with GSDMD and catalyzes its dimethylation at lysine 43. This modification promotes GSDMD cleavage by caspases, leading to increased oligomerization and membrane localization of GSDMD N-terminal fragment (GSDMD-NT), which ultimately induces pyroptosis. Disrupting or inhibiting SMYD3 alleviates overactivated inflammation, thereby protecting against lipopolysaccharide-induced death in mice and zebrafish. Our findings reveal a role for SMYD3 in regulating the inflammatory response and shed light on a new mechanism that modulates GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis.

articles_hidden.title: Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University
articles_hidden.authors: Gemma C. Solomon, George C. Schatz
articles_hidden.abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.

articles_hidden.title: Reply to Cirillo: Early-life exposure to the sugar-rationing regime, not a measured sugar dose, drives the cancer gradient
articles_hidden.authors: Chen Zhu, Weilong Zhang

articles_hidden.title: Ectopic expression of melanopsin promotes axonal regeneration in retinal ganglion cells via cAMP and TRPC signaling
articles_hidden.authors: Guang Li, Zuying Chai, Sonya Zhang, Yanxi Ren, King-Wai Yau, Sihan Li
articles_hidden.abstract: In mammals, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) show very minor axonal regeneration following axotomy. Despite genetic and pharmacological efforts to promote this regeneration, progress remains slow and limited, especially in overcoming potentially cell-type-specific barriers. In this paper, we virally expressed melanopsin (OPN4), which is the native photopigment in intrinsically-photosensitive RGCs (ipRGCs), broadly in RGCs. IpRGCs are known to show relative resistance to degeneration and axonal loss after injury. We correlated the exogenous-melanopsin-mediated intrinsic light responses of the successfully infected RGCs (referred to as +OPN4 RGCs) with their ability to show axonal regeneration after an optic-nerve crush. Specifically, we found +OPN4 RGCs to show functional rhabdomeric and ciliary motifs of phototransduction as we previously found in ipRGCs. +OPN4 αRGCs (the largest RGCs in the retina) exhibited light-triggered fast (via TRPC signaling) and slow (via cAMP signaling) response components, whereas +OPN4 non-αRGC responses comprised predominantly just a fast component. Genetic ablation of TRPC channels (TRPC6/7) or group II adenylyl cyclase (AC2/4/7) to abolish the fast or the slow response component, respectively, largely attenuated the axonal regeneration of +OPN4 αRGCs in the optic-nerve-crush model. At the same time, administration of cell-permeant cAMP not only rescued the AC2/4/7-knock-out phenotype in +OPN4 αRGCs but also potentiated axonal regeneration in some +OPN4 non-αRGCs, thus, possibly overcoming the potential subtype-specific barrier to axonal regeneration. Our results reveal an important role of joint TRPC- and cAMP-signaling in +OPN4 RGC axonal regeneration.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
articles_hidden.authors: David Aparicio, Juan R. Ortigosa, Kevin P. Guay, Robert V. Williams, Jorge O. Lannot, Guanghui Zong, Natalia Comino, José F. Rodríguez, Lai-Xi Wang, Marcelo A. Martí, Pietro Roversi, Daniel N. Hebert, Lila M. Gierasch, Carlos P. Modenutti, Marcelo E. Guerin
articles_hidden.abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

articles_hidden.title: Resource-driven release from lag phase triggers the world’s fastest and largest coastal plant invasion
articles_hidden.authors: Zhenpeng Ge, David M. Richardson, Petr Pyšek, Tinglu Cai, Yining Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: What determines the duration of invasion lag phases remains one of the major unresolved questions in invasion ecology. Lag phases are often attributed to genetic adaptation, propagule limitation, or demographic stochasticity, yet the mechanisms by which environmental conditions regulate establishment success remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the explosive expansion of Spartina alterniflora along the coast of mainland China, the most rapid plant invasion recorded globally. Combining field experiments, demographic theory, and historical invasion records, we identify resource-regulated Allee effects as a mechanism governing the invasion lag phase. Experimentally, sediment accretion substantially increases clonal propagation and sexual reproduction, weakening demographic constraints associated with establishment and accelerating the transition from sparse founder patches to highly reproductive meadows. A theoretical model reveals that sediment-driven positive feedbacks weaken demographic constraints during establishment and shorten the duration of Allee effects. Historical invasion records spanning both sides of the Pacific Ocean support the predicted negative relationship between sedimentation rate and lag-phase duration. Invasion lag phases can arise solely from interactions between species traits and environmental resource availability. Contrary to the prevailing view that Allee effects are fixed properties of species, our results show that their duration is regulated by environmental resource availability. More broadly, environmental resources can govern ecological transitions by controlling transient dynamics during establishment, providing an explanation for why some introduced populations remain dormant for decades, whereas others rapidly become dominant ecosystem engineers.

articles_hidden.title: An innervated and vascularized HNSCC-on-a-chip model built on defined and tunable engineered extracellular matrices
articles_hidden.authors: Alessia Maria Pignataro, Cornelia Christina Schwarz, Emilia Wiechec, Alessandro Cordiale, Shyama Sasikumar, Alexander Jenssen, Taka Ariyaberg, Lalit Pramod Khare, Ehsanul Hoque Apu, Karin Roberg, Sajjad Naeimipour, Gabriela Basile Carballo, Marcin Szczot, Daniel Aili, Marco Rasponi, Pierfrancesco Pagella
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding the tumor microenvironment requires experimental platforms that faithfully recapitulate its key components. Here, we present an innervated and vascularized head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)-on-a-chip platform built with fully defined and tunable engineered extracellular matrices (eECMs). In a stepwise increase of complexity, we first cocultured patient-derived HNSCC cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and endothelial cells within tailored eECMs, revealing extracellular matrix-dependent differences in transcriptional state, multicellular self-organization, and chemotherapeutic sensitivity. We then integrated these three-dimensional constructs into a cancer–vasculature interface, which enabled analysis of eECM-dependent directional collective migration and invasion. Finally, we incorporated trigeminal innervation through injectable 3D human bioengineered trigeminal ganglia, establishing a chip-based innervation–tumor–vasculature tri-interface. Together, this all-human platform integrates fully defined ECM, vasculature, and innervation in a single modular system to investigate tumor organization, invasion, and therapeutic responses within a controlled human microenvironment.

articles_hidden.title: C2CD3 links tooth patterning to evolutionary tooth loss in birds and dental anomalies across vertebrates
articles_hidden.authors: Piranit Kantaputra, Yeliz Guven, Narumon Bunpiem, Kimberly Cochran, Tengyang Qiu, Evan C. Brooks, Paisan Kangvonkit, Saisupee Arayasantiwong, Chumpol Ngamphiw, Sissades Tongsima, Puckpring Sompoprungroat, Nuttaporn Sengtae, Kanoknart Chintakanon, Saisinee Ngaohiranpat, Chidchanok Leetanakul, Stefan T. Arold, Tügba Kalayci, Katsushige Kawasaki, Atsushi Ohazama, Samantha A. Brugmann, Abigail S. Tucker
articles_hidden.abstract: Primary cilia play an essential role in molecular signaling transduction during development, coordinating cell fate decisions and morphogenesis. Defects in components of the primary cilium result in an array of developmental syndromes called ciliopathies. Here we report 24 patients with nine rare and seven novel variants in the primary cilia gene C2CD3, which has previously been implicated in the ciliopathy Orofaciodigital syndrome XIV. Patients displayed an array of dental defects impacting the number, shape, and timing of tooth development. To understand the etiology underlying these defects, murine and avian models were analyzed during embryonic development. Ap2Cre;C2cd3 ex4-5 fl/fl mouse mutants showed a range of dental defects prenatally, mimicking several of the phenotypes observed in patients. Shh was upregulated in the developing upper jaw, leading to a widening of the midline, while Shh expression in the lower jaw was reduced, highlighting the context-dependent impact of cilia on hedgehog signaling. In avian mutants carrying a C2CD3 variant, talpid 2 , tooth buds were evident with SHH expression upregulated during early development in both upper and lower jaws. Cartilage defects were additionally observed in both conditional mouse knockouts and talpid 2 embryos. These changes in Shh signaling provide a mechanism to explain the phenotypes in patients and highlight the conserved role of C2CD3 in coordinating the morphogenetic potential of the jaw and patterning of the forming dentition. Given the conserved phenotypes, alterations in C2CD3-dependent ciliogenesis may have played a role in modulating Shh signaling to alter the timing and position of tooth germs across vertebrate evolution.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial reorganization during post-collapse population growth suggests conspecific attraction in baleen whale nursing grounds
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Grundlehner, Virginia Andrews-Goff, Michael C. Double, Joshua N. Smith, Madeleine J. Brasier, Katherine A. Cresswell, Stuart P. Corney
articles_hidden.abstract: Habitat use is strongly interlinked with population dynamics and plays an important role in population regulation. Animals frequently modify their habitat use behavior in response to major changes in population density. This is well studied in contexts wherein resources are limiting: for example, when changes in habitat use behavior reduce pressure from resource limitations. Situations wherein resource limitations are relaxed, such as upon recovery from severe declines, remain poorly studied. Here, we study how the spatial distribution of a nearly extirpated animal population changed during population recovery. We study a population of southern right whales ( Eubalaena australis ), a migratory species that was nearly extirpated by whaling. Using large-scale annual aerial survey data (1976–2023), we assess how spatial distribution patterns at nursing grounds changed as annual coastal abundances grew from few individuals to a few hundred. This includes assessment of the species’ characteristic site fidelity at a uniquely large spatiotemporal scale. We observed weaker fidelity to specific sites than generally assumed for Australian southern right whales and found strong indications that conspecific attraction influences the species’ coastal habitat selection. Distribution patterns initially displayed strong dispersal but became increasingly clustered coincident with substantial growth in annual whale abundances. This transition captures a rare example of a population crossing a behavioral threshold, possibly reflecting a switch in behavioral strategy or lack of conspecific cues. Our findings suggest that the behavioral processes governing habitat selection can shift with population density, driving substantial reorganization of populations’ spatial structure during substantial demographic change.

articles_hidden.title: Protein resource allocation across subcellular compartments revealed by large-scale absolute quantitative proteomics in yeast
articles_hidden.authors: Hongzhong Lu, Zhendong Zhang, Siwei He, Yucan Zhang, Yuguang Wang, Fei Tao, Jens Nielsen
articles_hidden.abstract: Subcellular compartmentalization within complex membrane-bound organelles is a hallmark of eukaryal life, enabling metabolic specialization through spatial segregation. Here, we compiled a dataset encompassing 300 absolute quantitative proteomes, the largest to date, across two yeast species under diverse experimental conditions. Leveraging big data analysis, formula fitting, and machine learning, quantitative correlations among protein abundance, resource allocation, and cellular phenotypes were elucidated at a system level. We found that subcellular resource distribution is highly uneven and covaries with specific growth rate. Specifically, at high specific growth rates, the protein mass fraction (PMF) from certain compartments, (e.g., nucleus) is consistently reduced, coinciding with the increasing protein resource demand from ribosomes. Meanwhile, nutrient limitation may induce resource recycling by upregulating protein resources within specific compartments (e.g., vacuole) to sustain stress adaptation. Importantly, our integrative analysis indicates that PMF from a few subcellular compartments (e.g., nucleus and ribosomes) can accurately predict yeast physiological parameters (e.g., specific growth rate, oxygen uptake rate), and a limited protein set (≥ 23) could be used to capture the variation in resource allocation across seven major subcellular compartments. Furthermore, our comparative analysis between Crabtree-positive and Crabtree-negative species across conditions illustrates that subcellular resource allocation could be shaped by multiple factors and the two species differ markedly in their robustness to environmental perturbations. In summary, the high-quality quantitative proteomic dataset for yeast species offers an unprecedented opportunity for understanding the general principles underlying subcellular resource allocation, laying foundations for precision engineering of cell factories in synthetic biology.

articles_hidden.title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85
articles_hidden.authors: David C. Briggs, Ryan T. Duffy, Sarah Ateaque, Sarah Maslen, Hema Nagaraj, Yves-Alain Barde, Peter S. DiStefano, Ronald M. Lindsay, Paul C. Armstrong, Chloe J. Peach, Neil Q. McDonald
articles_hidden.abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.

articles_hidden.title: The ABCD hypothesis
articles_hidden.authors: William Chan
articles_hidden.abstract: If α and β are cardinals, then the cardinal exponentiation α β is the set of all functions from α into β . The ABCD hypothesis is the statement that for all infinite cardinals α ≤ β and γ ≤ δ , | α β | ≤ | γ δ | if and only if α ≤ γ and β ≤ δ . The Axiom of Determinacy, AD, states that every two-player infinite game on ω has a winning strategy for one of the two players. Let Θ be the supremum of the ordinals onto which R surjects. This paper will show that if AD holds and V = L ( R ) , then the ABCD hypothesis holds below Θ .

articles_hidden.title: Revised estimates of types and duration of long COVID symptoms based on claims records from 245 million US patients
articles_hidden.authors: Hamed Nilforoshan, Julia Reisler, Erfan Jahanparast, Michael Moor, Steven N. Goodman, Stefan Wager, Jure Leskovec
articles_hidden.abstract: COVID-19 has been reported to cause multisystem effects lasting years [Z. Al-Aly, E. Topol, Science 383, 830–832 (2024)]. These findings are primarily based on cohort studies comparing test-positive COVID-19 patients to controls without known COVID-19 infection, tested or untested [M. Cai, Y. Xie, E. J. Topol, Z. Al-Aly, Nat. Med. 30, 1564–1573 (2024)]. However, such comparisons can be biased by the reasons people were tested. Using 14.4 billion insurance claims from 244.7 million US patients, we find that most long-term effects attributed to COVID-19 by unrestricted control designs likely reflect bias due to selective testing of individuals with non-COVID conditions, causing long-term effects of those conditions to be misattributed to COVID-19. We removed this bias by analyzing only tested individuals, comparing test-positive to test-negative patients. Across 614 clinical outcomes followed over 2 y, the test-based design resulted in 83.5% fewer symptoms being attributable to COVID-19 between 30 to 119 d after infection (43 attributable symptoms vs. 262 for the unrestricted control design), a 98.2% reduction at 120 to 359 d (5 vs. 286), and a 100% reduction at 360 to 719 d (0 vs. 369). The unrestricted control design also attributed unrelated outcomes (e.g., firearm injuries) to COVID-19 at a high rate, whereas the testing-based design did not. The test-based control design may modestly underestimate some effects. This study does not indicate that symptoms beyond one year are not genuine but that their attributability to COVID-19 is uncertain.

articles_hidden.title: Rapid green leaf volatile sensing allows intact plants to release induced volatiles earlier than wounded emitters
articles_hidden.authors: Tristan M. Cofer, Lingfei Hu, Gaetan Glauser, Matthias Erb
articles_hidden.abstract: Organisms in the vicinity of attacked neighbors can respond to danger cues by activating their own defenses. However, the temporal dynamics of these interactions remain poorly resolved, despite their importance for the ensuing effects. Here, we investigated defense responses of maize plants that are exposed to induced volatiles from herbivory-induced neighbors in real time. These experiments revealed a surprising temporal paradox: Intact neighbors start emitting most induced volatiles 15 to 80 min earlier than the attacked plants themselves. This earlier responsiveness was not associated with earlier induction of defense hormones, volatile biosynthesis genes, or within-leaf volatile accumulation. Instead, receiver plants kept their stomata open, while attacked sender plants rapidly closed them, likely because of water loss. Using different volatile deficient mutants, we demonstrate that the rapid responses in receivers are triggered by green leaf volatiles, which are released from the wound sites of sender plants within minutes independently of stomatal aperture. Thus, nonattacked neighbors can act as “unhindered observers” that activate some defenses more quickly than attacked organisms themselves, as they do not have to deal with wound trauma. The resulting plant volatile concatenation patterns expand our understanding of volatile signaling and have the potential to shape population-level multitrophic interactions.

articles_hidden.title: Auxiliary BKβ4 subunits promote nanoscale coupling between BK and voltage-gated calcium channels
articles_hidden.authors: Aravind Kshatri, Luis O. Romero, Alberto J. Gonzalez-Hernandez, Alejandro Cerrada, Belinda Rivero-Pérez, David Bartolomé-Martín, Teresa Giraldez
articles_hidden.abstract: Intracellular Ca 2+ signals are essential for many cellular processes but must be tightly regulated to ensure precise spatial and temporal control. The large conductance calcium- and voltage-activated K + channel (BK) integrates intracellular Ca 2+ signaling and membrane depolarization to generate hyperpolarizing K + currents that regulate membrane excitability. In many cell types, BK channels achieve rapid activation through functional coupling with voltage-gated calcium (Ca V ) channels that provide localized Ca 2+ signals. However, the mechanisms that regulate the nanoscale organization of BK+Ca V channel complexes remain poorly understood. Here we investigated whether the BK auxiliary subunit β 4 (BKβ 4 ), which is widely expressed throughout the brain and modulates BK gating properties, influences the spatial organization and functional coupling of BK and Ca V channels. Using proximity ligation assays, electrophysiology, and superresolution stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we show that BKβ 4 promotes BK+Ca V nanodomain organization by increasing channel clustering and altering their spatial proximity at the plasma membrane. These structural changes enhance functional coupling between Ca 2+ influx and BK channel activation. Notably, the effects of BKβ 4 on nanodomain organization and coupling depend on the Ca V subtype involved. Together, our findings reveal that the BKβ 4 auxiliary subunit regulates the nanoscale architecture of BK+Ca V channel complexes and thereby modulates their functional interaction.

articles_hidden.title: Mechanically driven grain refinement in Mo by nanoindentation pop-ins: A case of transient instability
articles_hidden.authors: Feitao Li, Afnan Mostafa, Yaron Kauffmann, Niaz Abdolrahim, Eugen Rabkin
articles_hidden.abstract: During load-controlled nanoindentation of pristine metals, the homogeneous dislocation nucleation manifests as a sudden displacement burst, or pop-in, associated with shear stresses approaching the theoretical strength, massive dislocation nucleation, and rapid yet uncontrolled indenter penetration. Here, we show that manually terminating nanoindentation immediately after the first pop-in enables direct access to a transient deformation and reveals unexpected microstructural transformations in molybdenum (Mo). Using single-crystal Mo with different surface orientations, we demonstrate pop-in-induced nucleation of new, highly misoriented grains at room temperature. This nucleation behavior is attributed to two mechanically driven processes: 1) activation of twinning followed by the evolution of twin boundaries into random high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) and 2) rearrangement of dislocations into HAGBs within regions of high local dislocation density during the abrupt deformation accompanying the pop-in. Displacement-controlled atomistic simulations reproduce both twin- and dislocation-mediated grain nucleation within an individual grain when a preexisting grain boundary blocks dislocation glide. However, in the absence of such a grain boundary, nucleated dislocations glide into the surrounding crystal and fail to form new grains. Continued indentation beyond pop-in mechanically erases newly formed grains, as confirmed in both experiments and simulations, explaining why this phenomenon was not detected in previous studies. Together, the observed nucleation and subsequent erasure of the grains establish the nanoindentation pop-in as a simple, widely accessible platform for qualitatively probing transient microstructural evolution in defect-scarce metals.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting atmospheric sulfur chemistry: Acid-catalyzed pathways do not control H 2 SO 4 formation
articles_hidden.authors: Bo Long, Chaolu Xie, Joseph S. Francisco, Donald G. Truhlar
articles_hidden.abstract: Sulfuric acid (H₂SO 4 ) drives new particle formation and radiatively important aerosol processes in the atmosphere, but its formation pathways remain poorly resolved because of limited kinetics data. To clarify these pathways, we combined coupled-cluster calculations, reaction rate theory, and a global chemistry transport model to quantify acid-catalyzed SO 3 hydration and its atmospheric significance. We find that the overall kinetics is not governed by a tight transition state but rather is controlled by a preceding loose transition state associated with the formation of the precursor complex of the acid-catalyzed SO 3 hydration. Our results reverse a recent view that acid catalysis is the dominant contributor to atmospheric SO 3 hydration, instead supporting an earlier view that water catalysis dominates SO 3 hydration. Incorporating the revised kinetics into the GEOS-Chem atmospheric model reveals no significant impact of acid-catalyzed SO 3 hydration on the simulated concentrations of H 2 SO 4 . The present findings highlight the critical roles of variational transition states in kinetic modeling.

articles_hidden.title: Septin binding restricts Shigella growth and triggers intracellular tolerance
articles_hidden.authors: Gizem Özbaykal Güler, Chen Zhang, Dominik Brokatzky, Rajdeep Das, Richard Wheeler, Ivo Gomperts Boneca, Teresa Cortes, Suliana Manley, Serge Mostowy
articles_hidden.abstract: Pathogen survival relies on their ability to adapt to changing environments, yet how intracellular bacteria tolerate cell-autonomous immunity remains unclear. Septins assemble into cage-like structures around cytoplasmic Shigella targeted by autophagy, but their antibacterial activity was unknown. Using advanced microscopy and cell-free reconstitution, we show that septins polymerize into circumferentially oriented filaments that inhibit bacterial growth. RNA-sequencing reveals that septin binding to Shigella upregulates type III secretion system (T3SS) effectors and triggers a stress response. Underlying this, septin-bound Shigella possess hyperpolarized membranes, but without lethally damaged cell envelope. We show that exposure to septin binding enhances the impact of the cell envelope-targeting antibiotic polymyxin B. During infection, T3SS effector OspC1 prevents septin recruitment, while stress-response regulator cspC protects against septin-mediated changes to membrane potential. Hence, septin binding is intrinsically antibacterial and is sensed by Shigella as a danger signal to promote mechanisms of intracellular tolerance.

articles_hidden.title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating
articles_hidden.authors: Yaocai Liu, Rui He, Da Wei, Longfei Li, Mingcheng Yang, Junhua Yuan, Yi Peng
articles_hidden.abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system’s effective temperature with density.

articles_hidden.title: Spontaneous replication fork collapse regulates telomere length homeostasis in wild-type yeast
articles_hidden.authors: Margherita Paschini, Abigail E. Gillespie, Cynthia M. Reyes, Corinne A. McCoy, Karen A. Lewis, Leslie W. Glustrom, Tatyana O. Sharpee, Deborah S. Wuttke, Victoria Lundblad
articles_hidden.abstract: In most eukaryotes, the enzyme telomerase maintains the termini of linear chromosomes through the addition of repetitive telomeric sequences. It is widely assumed that the primary site of action for telomerase is the single-stranded G-rich overhang at the ends of linear chromosomes. However, increasing evidence indicates that a second telomerase substrate is generated in response to replication stress as the replisome traverses duplex telomeric DNA. We show here that this second substrate, created by spontaneous replication fork collapse in wild-type budding yeast, is elongated by telomerase at a much higher frequency than fully replicated chromosome termini. Furthermore, as much as ~200 nucleotides can be added in a single cell division to newly collapsed forks, indicating that replication fork collapse and the subsequent response by telomerase is a major determinant of telomere length homeostasis. This challenges a long-standing model which posits a length-sensing mechanism that assesses individual telomeres to determine whether yeast chromosome ends are in “telomerase-extendible” versus “telomerase-non-extendible” states. We propose that these two states are instead structurally and temporally distinct substrates for telomerase, generated by two different processes (fork collapse versus completion of DNA replication). We also show that fork collapse at telomeres is kept in check by a telomere-dedicated Cdc13/Stn1/Ten1 complex in collaboration with the canonical RPA complex, indicating that these two complexes stabilize single-stranded DNA exposed at the replication fork. Although failures during DNA replication are often genotoxic events, this represents an opposing example in which fork collapse has been co-opted to promote genome stability.

articles_hidden.title: Dlx1&2 directly promote expression of Cxcl14 to control synapse development and interneuron survival
articles_hidden.authors: Teng Guo, Susan Lindtner, Jia Sheng Hu, Siavash Fazel Darbandi, Yurong Wang, Emily Ling-Lin Pai, Athéna R. Ypsilanti, Cindy T. J. van Velthoven, Alex S. Nord, John L. R. Rubenstein
articles_hidden.abstract: Dlx genes have fundamental roles in the generation, differentiation, and functions of virtually all forebrain GABAergic neurons. Here we used scRNA-Seq to identify genes that are dysregulated in Dlx1/2 conditional mutants in mouse immature CGE- and MGE-derived cortical and olfactory bulb GABAergic interneurons. Dlx1/2 -regulated genes included Cxcl14 and Nr2f2 that are important for cortical interneuron (CIN) survival. We also identified DLX2-bound putative regulatory elements (pREs) of these Dlx -regulated genes. Within the Dlx -expressing lineage, some DLX-bound pREs were specific to CINs, others appeared to be constitutively bound; the latter class having activity in mature CINs. One such pRE and its associated gene, Cxcl14 , is strongly activated by Dlx1/2 and is essential for synaptogenesis onto CINs.

articles_hidden.title: Computation and sampling for Schubert specializations
articles_hidden.authors: David Anderson, Greta Panova, Leonid Petrov
articles_hidden.abstract: We study a problem at the interface of enumerative algebraic geometry, algebraic combinatorics, and the statistical mechanics of vertex models with long-range interactions. We develop methods to explore the values S w ( 1 , … , 1 ) of Schubert polynomials (called principal specializations), which count reduced bumpless pipe dreams (RBPDs) with boundary permutation w ∈ S n . We exhibit counterexamples to the conjecture of Merzon and Smirnov that S w ( 1 n ) is maximized on layered permutations; the smallest such example we find is at n = 17. Despite the counterexamples, we present bounds that support a refined conjecture that the maximum of S w ( 1 n ) over all w ∈ S n grows at the same asymptotic rate as the maximum over layered permutations (found by Morales, Pak, and Panova). We implement and benchmark four recurrences for Schubert specializations: the descent formula of Macdonald, the transition formula of Lascoux–Schützenberger, the cotransition formula of Knutson, and the formula of Billey, Jockusch, and Stanley. We also explore typical random permutations drawn with probability proportional to S w ( 1 n ) , equivalently from uniformly random RBPDs. Our simulations reveal a permuton-like limit analogous to the Grothendieck setting studied by Morales, Panova, Petrov, and Yeliussizov. For sampling, we show that the standard monotone Coupling From The Past framework does not apply to RBPDs, leaving exact uniform sampling open. To bypass this, we develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler augmented with macroscopic “droop” updates that preserve connectivity and accelerate mixing. Our publicly available fast implementations reach n = 20 for exact computation of S w ( 1 n ) and n = 100 for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling using a chain whose stationary distribution is uniform on RBPDs (run on a cluster).

articles_hidden.title: Orexin and pupillary modulation for hunger control
articles_hidden.authors: Seher Kosar, Eva Bracey, Nikola Grujic, Yihui Du, Daria Peleg-Raibstein, Denis Burdakov
articles_hidden.abstract: Fasting-based interventions improve metabolic health and are also explored as adjuncts in other clinical settings, but hunger remains a barrier to adherence. Fasting activates AgRP/NPY neurons (ANs), a hunger-promoting population whose inhibition reduces eating in hungry animals. Here we identify hypocretin/orexin neurons (HONs), classically associated with arousal, as rapid suppressors of AN activity. HON ablation increased AN population activity, whereas HON optostimulation rapidly suppressed it. Combined recordings of AN activity and pupil size—a direct arousal metric not previously linked to AN dynamics—revealed that HONs contributed to pupil dilation-associated AN suppression. In fasted mice, sensory stimulation rapidly recruited this pupil-HON pathway, and suppressed AN activity and eating. These findings reveal an arousal–hunger pathway through which self-initiated pupil dilations, or dilations driven by salient environmental events, interrupt fasting-induced hunger signals. They also suggest a framework for noninvasive, sensory-, and pupillometry-guided approaches to hunger control during fasting.

articles_hidden.title: Recognition-dependent activation of the Arabidopsis RRS1-R/RPS4 TIR-NLR immune receptor pair
articles_hidden.authors: Hee-Kyung Ahn, Guanghao Guo, Jan Skłenar, Shania Pin Yin Keh, Sung Un Huh, Michelle T. Hulin, Hayden Burdett, Maria Sindalovskaya, Seungjin Na, Jihyeon Choi, Nitika Mukhi, He Zhao, Lena S. Knorr, Eunok Paek, Mark J. Banfield, Frank L. H. Menke, Wenbo Ma, Jonathan D. G. Jones
articles_hidden.abstract: Plant TIR domain-containing proteins exhibit NADase activity upon pathogen effector recognition, creating small molecules that activate defense via EDS1 and its associated proteins. Arabidopsis RPS4 and RRS1 comprise a TIR-NLR immune receptor pair that recognizes multiple effector proteins including AvrRps4 and PopP2. We show here that RPS4 and RRS1 acquire NADase activity upon recognition of a cognate effector. However, both in the presence and absence of effector, RPS4 and RRS1 form an oligomer that does not change in size upon effector provision. Effector-dependent defense activation by RPS4 and RRS1 requires the catalytic glutamate residue and the BB-loop motif of RPS4, which is absent in RRS1 and other RRS1-like TIR domains in Arabidopsis . Oligomerization of RPS4 and RRS1 occurs through multiple domains, but oligomerization does not require enzymatic activity. We propose that conformational changes or reconfiguration within the RPS4/RRS1 oligomer upon effector recognition derepresses the complex for immune activation.
