articles_hidden.title: Imaging real-space chiral rotation of flat-band states in helical trilayer graphene
articles_hidden.authors: Chen-Yue Hao, Gengdong Zhou, Mo-Han Zhang, Zi-Han Guo, Zhida Song, Lin He
articles_hidden.abstract: Flat bands have been experimentally realized in a wide variety of graphene-based moiré systems with designed stacking configurations. While these moiré systems feature similar flat-band structures, they differ markedly in key characteristics, such as band flattening, band isolation, and band topology, which give rise to their distinct strongly correlated phases. Here, we present a systematic real-space investigation comparing flat-band states across four representative graphene moiré systems, revealing a characteristic chiral rotation of flat-band states within helical trilayer graphene. Using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, we directly observe that ultra-small twist-angle helical trilayer graphene unveils distinct threefold-anisotropic electronic states localized at certain moiré sites within the flat-band regime, distinguishing it from the other moiré systems investigated in this study. Spatial mapping of the threefold-anisotropic pattern reveals a chiral rotation that varies as a function of energy. Theoretical simulations based on the Bistritzer–MacDonald model reproduce the distinct orientations of the threefold-anisotropic patterns across different low-energy minibands and reveal a systematic correspondence between the direction of local density-of-states rotation and the structural chirality of helical trilayer graphene. Our results demonstrate that real-space electronic textures—previously overlooked—can partially reveal the intrinsic disparities among different flat bands, highlighting that systematic exploration of flat bands across moiré systems is critical for deciphering the origins of distinct correlated phases.

articles_hidden.title: Quantifying ancient architecture: Stone-level machine learning reveals architectural variation and settlement growth at Shivta
articles_hidden.authors: Erel Uziel, Gideon Avni, Gary M. Feinman, Guy Bar-Oz, Yitzchak Y. Jaffe
articles_hidden.abstract: Built environments provide durable evidence for how ancient settlements were organized, expanded, and transformed over time. Yet quantitative approaches to documenting architectural variability are generally labor-intensive, limited to individual structures, or dependent on aggregate volumetric estimates. We present a scalable, machine-learning-based framework that shifts the unit of analysis to the individual building stone and combines two complementary datasets: low-altitude drone imagery of surface remains and close-range photographs of standing walls. Applied to the Late Antique settlement of Shivta in the Negev Desert, the method automatically digitized approximately 235,000 surface stones and 12,000 stones in 604 walls, quantifying stone size, shape regularity, and masonry arrangement across walls, households, insulae, and the settlement as a whole. Higher masonry scores cluster around churches and parts of the settlement boundary, while the spatial distribution of masonry variation reveals a previously unidentified earlier boundary and provides evidence for outward expansion from a southern core. Combined with architectural sequencing, these patterns indicate the use of larger and more regularly shaped stones during Shivta’s principal phase of growth. The framework combines analytical flexibility with demonstrated robustness, supporting broader application across diverse stone-built archaeological contexts while complementing architectural energetics and enabling settlement-wide and cross-site comparisons of construction practices and settlement change.

articles_hidden.title: Ddx3x deficiency in mice impairs corticofugal motor circuits and causes motor deficits that are attenuated by early-life exercise
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren Dierdorff, Ikrame El Khaldi, Marta Garcia-Forn, Wei Wang, Jeronimo Lukin, Corinne M. Smith, Adele Mossa, Zhuhao Wu, Silvia De Rubeis
articles_hidden.abstract: The X-linked RNA helicase DDX3X is a high-risk gene for autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability primarily in females. Individuals with pathogenic variants in DDX3X have pervasive and often severe motor manifestations. Using mouse models, we studied the circuits underlying the motor phenotypes associated with Ddx3x deficiency and examined the feasibility of an early intervention to ameliorate motor trajectories. We show that Ddx3x controls both the development and later plasticity of motor circuits connecting the motor cortex with the pontine nuclei. Ddx3x haploinsufficiency during development affects the dendritic arborization of corticopontine neurons. Juvenile-onset Ddx3x loss in corticopontine neurons is sufficient to induce adult motor impairments overlapping with those caused by chemogenetic disruption of corticopontine circuits. Further, Ddx3x mutant mice engage corticopontine circuits in skilled motor tasks in a sex-dependent manner. Last, Ddx3x haploinsufficient female mice undergoing a juvenile motor intervention show long-lasting specific benefits in their adult motor function. Together, these findings establish Ddx3x as an essential regulator of corticopontine neuron development and function and provide an early motor intervention to ameliorate motor outcomes in a mouse model of DDX3X haploinsufficiency.

articles_hidden.title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders
articles_hidden.authors: Nadja Geiger, Maxim Q. Capelle, Phillip Rosentreter, Marie E. Herberstein, Armin Bahl, Massimo De Agrò, Barrett A. Klein, Daniela C. Rößler
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental behavioral state found across the animal kingdom, yet most of what we know about sleep is heavily vertebrate-biased. Studies are scarce or nonexistent in all but a few invertebrate lineages. A recent study of an REM sleep-like behavior in a jumping spider has reported unexpected parallels to sleep expression in vertebrates. So far, experimental evidence that these behavioral indicators truly represent sleep was lacking in spiders. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into sleep behavior in the spider Portia fimbriata (Salticidae). We demonstrate diurnal activity, a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM-like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption. We conclude that the behavior we observe in spiders is behavioral sleep, providing evidence for an REM-like sleep substate in a terrestrial invertebrate. These results contribute to fundamental questions about the evolution and function of sleep across animals.

articles_hidden.title: Neuromodulation-inspired gated associative memory networks: Extended memory retrieval and emergent multistability
articles_hidden.authors: Daiki Goto, Hector Manuel Lopez Rios, Monika Scholz, Suriyanarayanan Vaikuntanathan
articles_hidden.abstract: Classical autoassociative memory models have been central to understanding emergent computations in recurrent neural circuits across diverse biological contexts. However, they typically neglect neuromodulatory agents that are known to strongly shape memory capacity and stability. Here we introduce a minimal, biophysically motivated associative memory network in which neuromodulator-like signals are modeled by a self-adaptive, activity-dependent gating mechanism. Using many-body simulations and dynamical mean-field theory, we show that such gating fundamentally reorganizes the attractor structure: the network bypasses the classical spin-glass transition, maintaining robust, high-overlap retrieval far beyond the standard critical capacity. Mechanistically, when the gates act as fully open or fully closed switches, the gate stabilizes transient “ghost” remnants of stored patterns even far above the Hopfield limit, converting a single memory fixed-point attractor into a cluster of fixed points. The retrieved state is set by the initial overlap rather than quantized to the stored pattern. This graded dependence may be exploited for input-driven computation with persistent activity. These results establish that neuromodulation-like gating alone—without modifying synaptic weights or introducing explicit higher-order couplings—can dramatically expand memory capacity, eliminate catastrophic breakdown, and reshape a discrete attractor landscape into a rich continuum, suggesting a general and biologically accessible route to enhanced computational capabilities in neural circuits and neuromorphic architectures.

articles_hidden.title: Synchronous end-Permian mass extinction zenith in marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial North China
articles_hidden.authors: Hongliang Lu, Baochun Huang, Mingsong Li, Qian Zhao, Xiang Li, Yilian Liao, Zhaowen Pei, Yi Xue, Josep M. Parés, Haotian Zhang, Qingqing Jiang
articles_hidden.abstract: The end-Permian mass extinction was the most severe biotic crisis of the Phanerozoic, yet temporal synchrony between marine and terrestrial extinctions remains debated due to correlation uncertainties. Here, we present an integrated magnetostratigraphic, cyclostratigraphic, and carbon-isotope and mercury (Hg) chemostratigraphic record from the fluvial Upper Shihhotse, Sunjiagou, and Liujiagou formations at the Sigou section, North China. We identify 14 magnetozones spanning the late Changhsingian to late Olenekian, constrained by a floating timescale based on gamma-ray cyclostratigraphy and subsequently anchored through magnetostratigraphic correlation. Our chronostratigraphy reveals a Hg peak at 252.4 Ma, aligning with the main eruptive phase of the Siberian Traps Large Igneous Province, while the carbon isotope excursion onset (252.1 Ma) and minimum (252.0 Ma) are synchronous with the Meishan Global Stratotype Section and Point. Furthermore, the Induan–Olenekian boundary is positioned below magnetozone SG4n, constraining the Induan Stage duration to 1.6 to 1.8 My. These findings establish a high-resolution chronostratigraphic framework for the Permian–Triassic boundary in North China, supporting a synchronous extinction zenith across marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial ecosystems, with latitudinal diachroneity relative to high-latitude and tropical landmasses.

articles_hidden.title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Rao, Konstantinos Manos, Tuo Zhao, Minjie Chen, Glaucio H. Paulino
articles_hidden.abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence and gaps in the proposed ALDH9A1–carnitine–acetyl-CoA–IL-1β axis
articles_hidden.authors: Tao Yu, Wanjun Yu

articles_hidden.title: Stress-inducible WASF3 regulates brain metabolism and cognitive function
articles_hidden.authors: Abu M. Syed, Jin Ma, Ping-yuan Wang, Youlim Son, Rozhin Penjweini, Nikhil Mattu, Jay R. Knutson, Sachiko Nakamori-Yamashita, Danielle A. Springer, Ananya Ganguly, Chengyu Liu, Paul M. Hwang
articles_hidden.abstract: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein family member 3 (WASF3) disrupts mitochondrial respiration and is induced in association with endoplasmic reticulum stress in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Because cognitive impairment is a hallmark of ME/CFS, we investigated the role of WASF3 in brain metabolism and function using WASF3 transgenic and knockout mouse models. WASF3 disrupted respiratory complex IV and localized to mitochondria-associated membranes, known to modulate cellular processes important for neuronal activity. Overexpression of WASF3 in the hippocampus, a critical region for memory formation, induced a metabolic shift toward glycolysis and promoted a “hypometabolic” state. Increased WASF3 also caused a reduction in ATPIF1, previously shown to facilitate cognitive function, and impaired learning. Conversely, WASF3 deficiency increased ATPIF1 level, enhanced oxidative metabolism, and preserved cognitive function under stress. Together, these findings demonstrate that WASF3 suppresses oxidative metabolism in the brain and contributes to cognitive dysfunction, providing mechanistic insights into the “brain fog” reported in ME/CFS.

articles_hidden.title: DCAF6 reprograms TGF-β responses through TRIM33 destruction
articles_hidden.authors: Hongjie Luo, Bo Yuan, Jinquan Liu, Zeda Yao, Huanyu Hong, Dachuan Lin, Shuyi Zhang, Jiayi Qian, Jie Li, Jin Cao, Xia Lin, Bin Zhao, Pinglong Xu, Carl-Henrik Heldin, Jianping Jin, Yi Yu, Xin-Hua Feng
articles_hidden.abstract: TGF-β signaling plays a pivotal role in regulating numerous cellular processes, primarily through the Smad-dependent pathway. Disruptions of the pathway are associated with developmental disorders and life-threatening diseases, such as cancer. It has been reported that TRIM33 inactivates Smad4 signaling and also drives its own signaling responses. However, the mechanism controlling TRIM33 activity has remained unclear. In this study, we identify DCAF6 as a previously unrecognized ubiquitin ligase for TRIM33. DCAF6 targets TRIM33 at Lys850 for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation, thus abolishing TRIM33-mediated mono-ubiquitination of Smad4. As such, DCAF6 induces dual consequences: it enhances Smad4-dependent transcriptional and growth inhibitory responses, while simultaneously eliminating TRIM33-dependent developmental responses. Conversely, DCAF6 knockout suppresses Smad4-dependent responses while amplifying TRIM33-dependent responses. Therefore, DCAF6 operates as a critical regulator in the balance of TGF-β signaling between the Smad4 and TRIM33 pathways. These insights deepen our understanding of the dynamics and fate control of TGF-β signaling and may open avenues for therapeutic approaches targeting TGF-β in diseases.

articles_hidden.title: A spatially deployable iron redox rheostat tunes root growth under nutritional stress
articles_hidden.authors: Joaquín Clúa, Ana Berbel, Cristina Urbez, Francisco Madueño, Yves Poirier, Miguel A. Blázquez
articles_hidden.abstract: Root growth must continuously adjust to fluctuating nutrient availability, yet the mechanisms that quantitatively integrate environmental signals into developmental responses remain poorly understood. Distinct nutrient stresses, including ammonium toxicity and phosphate deficiency, inhibit primary root growth through iron-dependent processes, suggesting that iron acts as a central regulatory node. Here, we show that plants use an antagonistic module composed of CYBDOM ferrireductases and LPR ferroxidases to regulate apoplastic iron homeostasis and control root growth in a graded manner. Genetic perturbation of this module demonstrates that root growth inhibition scales quantitatively with iron accumulation, supporting a proportional control mechanism rather than a binary response. Loss of CYBDOM function causes excessive iron accumulation, elevated reactive oxygen species, and impaired meristem activity, whereas increased CYBDOM activity buffers iron deposition and confers resistance to stress. Mechanistically, iron-induced oxidative stress promotes HYP1 expression, which in turn limits further iron accumulation. Transcriptomic analyses distinguish ammonium-specific responses from Fe-associated transcriptional changes enriched in redox buffering and cell-wall remodeling. Finally, we show that this regulatory module is redeployed in distinct tissues under phosphate deficiency, indicating that plants reuse a conserved iron-based mechanism to coordinate growth across environmental contexts. Together, our findings establish genetically controlled Fe accumulation as a key determinant of developmental plasticity under nutrient stress.

articles_hidden.title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes
articles_hidden.authors: Dave Speijer
articles_hidden.abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont’s electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.

articles_hidden.title: Position-specific isotope signatures evolve during a reversible reaction
articles_hidden.authors: Cornelia Rasmussen, David W. Hoffman
articles_hidden.abstract: Position-specific isotope distributions capture information about reaction dynamics, metabolism, and environmental processes, encoding the formation history of organic molecules. Kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects are fundamental drivers of isotope fractionation, yet how these effects are expressed in position-specific isotope distributions remains poorly constrained. Here, we use glucose mutarotation as a model reaction for tracking the evolution of position-specific isotope ratios in a system in disequilibrium. In aqueous solution, α- and β-glucose interconvert through a low-abundance open-chain intermediate, providing an ideal framework for probing isotope effects within a single molecular pool at natural 13 C abundance. Using NMR spectroscopy, we simultaneously measure glucose anomer populations and position-specific 13 C/ 12 C ratios, enabling direct, time-resolved observations of isotope fractionation at the anomeric (C1) carbon. Starting from α-glucose, initial β-glucose formation generates a large transient isotope disequilibrium driven by unequal forward and reverse kinetic isotope effects, producing a temporary divergence in 13 C abundance of more than 30‰ between anomers. Continued interconversion redistributes the isotopes and yields an equilibrium difference of ~7‰ between α- and β-glucose at the C1 position. Together, these results demonstrate how kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects acting within a reversible reaction can generate substantial, time-dependent intramolecular isotope heterogeneity, with potential implications for how position-specific isotope signatures emerge and propagate through (biogeochemical) reaction networks.

articles_hidden.title: Autonomous disproofs of the Erdős unit distance conjecture with GPT-5.5 Pro
articles_hidden.authors: Yichen Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: OpenAI’s disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marks a milestone in AI for mathematical research. However, the result relied on an internal model with undisclosed test-time compute, hindering independent reproduction and analysis by the community. Here we present a simple autonomous agent built on the publicly available GPT-5.5 Pro. The agent uses a problem-agnostic three-stage prompting pipeline: brainstorm, execute, and review. We ran eight independent trials with web search disabled. In each trial, the agent produced a correct or essentially correct disproof of the conjecture. The resulting proofs are diverse and do not merely reproduce earlier AI-generated proofs. Since GPT-5.5 Pro was released nearly a month before OpenAI published its disproof, our evaluation is free from data contamination. The system operates efficiently, using an average of 106.7 k reasoning tokens per trial. We release our code and all outputs, providing a publicly accessible AI agent to resolve this conjecture autonomously.

articles_hidden.title: Defining and measuring proximity to criticality based on univariate time series
articles_hidden.authors: J. Samuel Sooter, Antonio J. Fontenele, Andrea K. Barreiro, Cheng Ly, Keith B. Hengen, Woodrow L. Shew
articles_hidden.abstract: Diverse social, engineered, and biological systems are made up of multiple interacting dynamical components; to work properly, certain components must be carefully regulated so that their dynamics avoid instability. However, many desirable properties, like optimized computation and control, emerge close to the tipping point between stability and instability, i.e., near criticality. Claims that such dynamical systems operate near criticality have been controversial because it is difficult to assess proximity to criticality when control parameters are unknown, hard to manipulate experimentally, and fluctuating in response to changing environmental or internal conditions. Moreover, observations of system dynamics are often limited to time series measurements of one or a few components. Here we develop a temporal renormalization group theory for defining criticality for univariate time series models and an information theoretic definition of proximity to criticality that is independent of model parameterization. We apply this theory to order-n autoregressive models resulting in a data-analytic strategy for time-resolved estimates of proximity to criticality based on measured univariate time series. After benchmarking our approach on diverse ground-truth cases, we apply it to recordings of spiking activity in the mammalian brain. Our estimate of proximity to criticality predicts behavior and suggests that brain dynamics shift closer to criticality during wakefulness and shift away during deep sleep.

articles_hidden.title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Hilbert
articles_hidden.abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: Viral metagenomics reveals heterogeneity in mammalian virus hosting, sharing, and spillover
articles_hidden.authors: Yuhao Wang, Guanyu Qu, Zheng Y. X. Huang, Xinyu Zhang, Hongfeng Li, Xuemin Wei, Li Hu, Shixia Xu, Daniel J. Becker, Fuwen Wei, Yifei Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: Zoonotic viruses originating from mammals pose a persistent threat to global health. While rodents and bats are often considered “special reservoirs,” it is debated if spillover risk is driven by specific taxa or merely reflects mammalian species richness. However, most tests have focused on published host–virus association datasets, which can reflect systematic biases in host and virus sampling effort. To address this limitation, we analyzed a comprehensive repository of 4,685 metagenomic datasets, minimizing bias toward any one viral taxon and spanning 296 species across 14 mammalian orders. We characterized the global mammalian virome and found substantial heterogeneity in the capacity of different mammalian orders to harbor and share human-associated viruses. Counter to conventional wisdom, carnivores exhibited significantly higher propensities to carry human-associated viruses, with bats ranked lower in this metric of zoonotic risk. Network analyses of viral sharing further revealed higher cross-order virus sharing among specific mammalian orders (e.g., carnivores and artiodactyls). Phylogenetic comparative analyses revealed that host life-history traits (e.g., longevity) and anthropogenic factors (e.g., urban land use) were key ecological drivers of both virus richness and transmission centrality. Our study provides a data-driven framework that challenges prevailing narratives of zoonotic risk and offers a refined strategy for prioritizing surveillance and mitigating emerging zoonotic threats.

articles_hidden.title: Direct atomic-scale observation reveals rare earth element fractionation at mineral–water interfaces
articles_hidden.authors: Lingyu Ran, Gaofeng Wang, Jianxi Zhu, Bowen Ling, Jie Xu, Xiangwei Zhang, Xiaoliang Liang, Yongqiang Yang, Jingming Wei, Hongping He
articles_hidden.abstract: Clay minerals, ubiquitous across diverse geological systems, exert fundamental controls on critical geochemical processes, particularly through their adsorptive interactions with economically vital elements such as heavy rare earth elements (HREEs). The adsorption of HREEs onto clay surfaces is not only the key process that enriches these critical resources but also a potential archive for dating significant weathering events. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing the preferential adsorption and fractionation of rare earth elements (REEs) at mineral–water interfaces have remained poorly constrained. Here, employing in situ atomic-scale imaging via high-resolution atomic force microscopy, we systematically investigate the adsorption behaviors of light and heavy REEs (La, Y, Yb) onto key crystallographic planes—Si-basal, Al-basal, and edge terminations—of representative clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, mica) under environmentally relevant conditions (pH 4.8 to 6.4). We directly visualize and quantitatively reveal that Si-basal planes selectively enrich HREEs with pH-enhanced adsorption capacity, whereas Al-basal planes exhibit negligible REE adsorption below pH 5.8 but preferential HREE adsorption at pH 6.4. Integrating synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the adsorption mechanism of REE on Si-basal and Al-basal/edge planes as outer-sphere complexation and inner-sphere binding, respectively. Furthermore, we quantify the contributions of distinct planes via surface complexation modeling, revealing Si-dominated to Al- and edge-controlled adsorption with elevating pH. These atomic-scale findings not only resolve long-standing debates about clay mineral-mediated REE fractionation but also redefine fundamental paradigms of surface reactivity at silicate mineral–water interfaces, offering insights into the cycling and metallogeny of other critical metals in aqueous and sedimentary environments.

articles_hidden.title: Solid-state laser refrigeration of nanoscale quantum sensors
articles_hidden.authors: Zhaojie Feng, Anupum Pant, Robert G. Felsted, Alexander B. Bard, Xiaojing Xia, Siamak Dadras, Kamran Shayan, Danika R. Luntz-Martin, Donald Mannikko, Lars Forberger, Alexey Soldatenko, Ilia M. Pavlovetc, Stefan Stoll, Masaru Kuno, A. Nickolas Vamivakas, Peter J. Pauzauskie
articles_hidden.abstract: Photothermal heating remains a major challenge during the optical excitation of nanoscale quantum sensors [C. Bradac, S. F. Lim, H. C. Chang, I. Aharonovich, Adv. Opt. Mater. 8 , 2000183 (2020)]. At low laser powers, heating of the sensor leads to the thermal drift of quantum electronic transition energies. At high laser powers, sensors degrade due to thermally induced phase transitions, including melting. Here, we report a general approach for mitigating the photothermal heating of nanoscale quantum sensors through solid-state laser refrigeration of the sensors’ underlying substrate. Experimentally, both nanodiamonds and gold nanocrystals are attached separately to a ceramic laser-cooling substrate through van der Waals interaction. A combination of Debye–Waller factor thermometry and optically detected magnetic resonance spectroscopy of nitrogen vacancy centers is used to demonstrate that solid-state laser refrigeration of the substrate can reduce the temperature of attached nanodiamond payloads by 25 ± 3 K below steady-state operating temperatures. Stokes/anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy is used to demonstrate reduced photothermal heating of plasmonic gold nanocrystals by 8.8 ± 2.7 K during surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy sensing of rhodamine-6G molecules. These results suggest that solid-state laser cooling could open up experimental possibilities for rapid feedback-controlled cooling of a wide range of nanoscale quantum resources.

articles_hidden.title: Profile of Barbara Sherwood Lollar
articles_hidden.authors: Tinsley H. Davis
articles_hidden.abstract: In a laboratory nearly 2.4 kilometers under the Canadian Shield, geochemist Barbara Sherwood Lollar has tracked the sustained release of enough hydrogen gas from Earth’s crust to produce 4.7 million kilowatt-hours of energy per year. Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2022, Sherwood Lollar revisited the Kidd Creek Mine in Ontario, Canada where, in 2013, her explorations found that waters flowing from deep fractures were 1.6 billion years old. Reported in her Inaugural Article, the findings, aided by studies of noble gases in the samples, pushed the age of Earth’s oldest waters back by hundreds of millions of years.

articles_hidden.title: Lysine crotonylation acts as an epigenetic switch for glutamate neurotransmission and spatial memory
articles_hidden.authors: Utsav Mukherjee, Budhaditya Basu, Pratyush Suryavanshi, Stacy E. Beyer, Saaman Ghodsi, Nathan Robillard, Yann Vanrobaeys, Eric B. Taylor, Joseph Glykys, Ted Abel, Snehajyoti Chatterjee
articles_hidden.abstract: Histone posttranslational modifications, particularly lysine acetylation (Kac), are critical epigenetic regulators of transcriptional programs underlying long-term memory consolidation. Beyond Kac, several other non-acetyl acylations have been identified with the ability to regulate transcription; however, their role in memory consolidation remains unknown. Here, we identify histone lysine crotonylation (Kcr) as a molecular switch for long-term memory and glutamatergic neurotransmission. We find that spatial learning induces distinct spatiotemporal patterns of Kcr across hippocampal subregions. Through genetic manipulations, we show that reducing hippocampal Kcr levels impairs memory, while increasing Kcr levels by means of crotonate administration enhances long-term memory. Single-nuclei transcriptome and chromatin accessibility analyses reveal that crotonate facilitates activation of genes regulating glutamate signaling. Cell–cell communication analysis further suggests a strengthening of glutamatergic signaling within hippocampal excitatory neurons following crotonate administration. Real-time fluorescence imaging with genetically encoded sensors functionally validates our multiomics and computational findings—demonstrating the role of Kcr in regulating presynaptic glutamate release and neuronal activity. In summary, our findings elucidate a key mechanism underlying long-term memory consolidation and excitatory neurotransmission, linking epigenetic events to synaptic function and behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Hepatitis C viral variants bear signatures of de novo CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure after spontaneous postpartum viral suppression
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher C. Phelps, Stephanie Smith, John Gridley, Jennifer A. Kohout, Zhaohui Xu, Joseph Marcotrigiano, Kara Rood, Nicole E. Skinner, Arash Grakoui, Jonathan R. Honegger, Christopher M. Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: Progression to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection entails loss of HCV-specific CD4+ T cell help, emergence of viral variants that escape recognition by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies, and exhaustion of CD8+ T cells targeting remaining intact epitopes. Once chronic infection has been established, it is generally lifelong without treatment. However, in some chronically infected women, a surprising postpartum viral load decline has been linked to resurgent functional HCV-specific CD4+ helper T cells. A minority of women even spontaneously clear long-standing chronic infection postpartum. To test whether restored T cell help boosts HCV-specific CD8+ T cell or antibody responses in women with postpartum viral control, we performed serial near-full-length deep sequencing of HCV genomes to assess evolution of viral MHC class I epitopes and antibody epitopes in nine women with significant postpartum viral declines (≥ 1 log 10 at 3 mo postpartum, “controllers”) and 12 with more stable levels (“noncontrollers”). Although not associated with mutations arising early postpartum, at 12 to 24 mo postpartum, viral control was strongly associated with amino acid mutations in epitopes predicted to be targeted by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies. Plasma from controllers also demonstrated a postpartum increase in neutralization of multiple HCV strains. Together, these findings support the hypothesis that postpartum viral control is mediated by CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure.

articles_hidden.title: Prioritize validation over discovery of novel antibiotics
articles_hidden.authors: Mark A. Hanson, Thomas C. G. Bosch, Irene A. Chen, Michael Zasloff

articles_hidden.title: Hydration at the base of the mantle transition zone by ancient subductions in Asia
articles_hidden.authors: Jiyu Liu, Wenzhong Wang, Wenjiao Xiao, Zhu Mao, Yajie Zhao, Zhongqing Wu
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine–Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol–Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth’s deep water cycle.

articles_hidden.title: Potential energy landscape networks of confined vortex matter
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Wenzhao Li, Dipanjan Ray, Zoltán Toroczkai, Boldizsár Jankó
articles_hidden.abstract: Advances in nanoscale patterning of superconducting films [Y. L. Wang et al ., Nat. Nanotechnol. 13 , 560–565 (2018)] and the availability of submicron-sized superconducting single crystals with controlled geometry allow for the investigation of superconducting vortex matter under extreme confinement [A. K. Geim et al ., Nature 390 , 259–262 (1997)]. It has been observed in these systems that the interplay between sample geometry and vortex number results in the emergence of so-called “magic number” configurations which show unusually high stability against thermal fluctuations. However, a detailed, comprehensive theoretical study of the ground state and metastable states of confined vortex matter has not yet been developed. Here we show that the intricate properties of a system of vortices under extreme confinement can be characterized in detail by mapping the potential energy landscape of the system onto a network [J. P. K. Doye, Phys. Rev. Lett. 88 , 238701 (2002)] with nodes corresponding to local potential energy minima and edges to transition states between local minima. We apply these techniques to systems featuring repelling particles/vortices confined in small containers of various geometric shapes. We demonstrate that the ground state almost always belongs to a subset of system states within the deepest network core. We find that the emergence of magic number configurations in the ground state results in a drastic decrease in the complexity of the entire network. We use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to study the size dependence of melting in different configurations. We find that as confinement effects increase, magic number configurations transition to states with lower symmetry.

articles_hidden.title: Sources and sinks: Geoclimatic dynamics shaped the assembly of endemic fauna in the world’s Third Pole
articles_hidden.authors: Dechun Jiang, Mao-Liang Li, Jin-Long Ren, Rui-Han Li, Zhi-Tong Lyu, Sebastian Klaus, Ru-Wan Jia, Tao Xue, Jia-Tang Li
articles_hidden.abstract: The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), a biodiversity hotspot shaped by tectonic and climatic forces, has seen significant progress in understanding its floristic origins. However, a comprehensive, multitaxon perspective on how its terrestrial fauna assembled remains lacking. Here we integrate time-calibrated phylogenies of over 20,000 species from five major groups (invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals), to reconstruct the evolutionary history of 527 terrestrial animal species endemic to the QTP. Our finding reveals that the QTP has functioned both as a center of in situ diversification and as a “biogeographic sink” that receives species from surrounding regions, however, with pronounced subregional differentiation: the Hengduan Mountains acted primarily as a diversification source, while the Himalaya and the Plateau Platform acted as sinks, accumulating lineages from adjacent regions. The Eocene–Oligocene climatic transition, rather than late Neogene uplift, initiated sustained faunal diversification and biotic exchange. Across subregions, distinct uplift histories and monsoon regimes drove asynchronous evolutionary trajectories, showing that even geographically adjacent regions can exhibit distinct accumulation patterns of lineages. Notably, integrating our faunal evidence with recent floristic assembly data reveals a consistent “plants first, animals later” pattern across the QTP and its subregions, suggesting that early-arriving plant lineages created ecological niches that facilitated subsequent faunal colonization and diversification. This framework advances our understanding of how mountain biotas assemble over time, with implications extending far beyond the QTP.

articles_hidden.title: Decoding climate anomalies—From scientifically sound to societally relevant
articles_hidden.authors: Molly E. Brown, Elena Tarnavsky, Markus Enenkel
articles_hidden.abstract: As climate impacts worsen, decision-makers, researchers, and public sector institutions increasingly need reliable, relevant, and appropriate information about emerging weather and climate anomalies. However, with the ever-expanding choice of datasets based on ground observations, satellite data, and models, it is critical to not only use the best dataset for a specific decision-making need but to avoid misinforming and even derailing decision-making due to dataset selection. The main objective of this perspective is to illustrate the importance of understanding datasets used to translate climate data into actionable knowledge, supporting the next generation of science- and data-driven climate risk management instruments, projects, and global initiatives. Through the lens of three use cases, we illustrate what data quality means for different applications, the implications of choosing, aggregating, and combining different climate datasets, and the potential consequences of dataset and baseline choice on decision-making. Choosing different datasets often leads to trade-offs that decision-makers need to be aware of, for instance, between the spatial resolution of a dataset and length of the data record. Here, we discuss the implications of selecting the appropriate time step, resolution, and dataset and provide examples of how these choices affect the identification of societally relevant anomalies.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluation of possibly fabricated references in 500,000 science, engineering, and computing papers
articles_hidden.authors: Maxim Topaz, Pallavi Gupta, Zhihong Zhang, Laura-Maria Peltonen
articles_hidden.abstract: References to nonexistent studies are well documented in biomedical research, but evidence outside biomedicine is limited. We analyzed a stratified random sample of 500,000 peer-reviewed journal papers in chemistry, physics, materials science, engineering, and computer science published from January 2023 through March 31, 2026, using OpenAlex, a large open index of scholarly works and citations. Our automated pipeline classified 1,135 references across 619 papers as fabricated, with 85.8% precision on masked expert review; fabricated is an operational label for a claimed title that could not be located in any of seven bibliographic and open-web sources. Affected-paper prevalence rose from 1 in 1,600 (6.3 per 10,000) in 2023 to 1 in 435 (23.0 per 10,000) in the first quarter of 2026, and full-period rates differed roughly sixfold across fields, from 25.6 per 10,000 papers in physics to 4.3 in chemistry. Most affected papers contained one or two fabricated references, but the 27 papers containing five or more accounted for more than a third of all fabricated references identified. Applying each field’s rate to the approximately 7 million OpenAlex papers indexed in these fields gives an estimated 8,500 papers carrying at least one fabricated reference. Routine automated reference verification at submission, together with retrospective screening of the published literature, can detect fabricated references before and after they enter the scientific record.

articles_hidden.title: The lncRNA-encoded micropeptide ANCHOR promotes lateral root growth and drought tolerance in rice
articles_hidden.authors: Rui-Rui He, Jie Jiang, Chao Yuan, Xing-Lan Cao, Kai-Bin Peng, Nan Zhang, Lan-Jun Luo, Chuan-Ying Fang, Zhi-Yu Zhang, Xin-Ya Niu, Wen-Hui Li, Wan-Ting Mo, Yu-Hong Liao, Qing Liu, Yu-Chan Zhang, Jian-Ping Lian, Yu Cheng, Yue-Qin Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Lateral roots (LRs) are important components of plant root systems, determining the robustness of root system architecture and influencing water uptake efficiency. Enhancing the phenotypic plasticity of LRs is key to improving crop production under fluctuating environmental conditions. In this study, we identified ANCHOR, a micropeptide encoded by a long noncoding RNA that is predominantly expressed in LR primordia and plumules. Overexpression of ANCHOR resulted in significantly longer and wider LRs, thereby altering root system architecture and enhancing drought tolerance; knockouts of ANCHOR produced the opposite phenotypes. Mechanistically, ANCHOR localized to plastids and directly interacted with the lysine biosynthetic enzyme LL-diaminopimelate aminotransferase 1 (LL-DAPAT). Our results indicate that ANCHOR functions as a “molecular glue” that enhances DAPAT dimerization. Through its influence on lysine metabolism, ANCHOR raises the levels of the auxin biosynthetic precursor tryptophan, thereby affecting auxin homeostasis. These findings show that lncRNA-derived micropeptides, like their precursor RNAs, can function as fine-tuning regulators. This function of micropeptides, together with their small molecular size, may make them suitable for application as bioeffectors to stimulate root growth and improve plant tolerance to abiotic stress without side effects for plants.

articles_hidden.title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
articles_hidden.authors: Steven K. Chen, Jing Liu, Belinda S. W. Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

articles_hidden.title: The scope and severity of bat fatalities at US wind energy facilities
articles_hidden.authors: Charles J. Labuzzetta, Ashton M. Wiens, Bradley J. Udell, Teresa F. Bohner, Jay E. Diffendorfer, Alejandro Grajal-Puche, Cris D. Hein, Arnold E. Johnsen, Anthony Lopez, Trieu Mai, Brian E. Reichert, Megan M. Seymour, Wayne E. Thogmartin, Bethany R. Frid
articles_hidden.abstract: Wind turbines are a major source of bat fatalities in the United States, yet the magnitude and species-specific patterns of these fatalities have remained poorly quantified because monitoring has been site-specific, unstandardized, and not designed for landscape-level synthesis. In the most comprehensive analysis to date, we synthesized 499 postconstruction monitoring reports and developed a multispecies Bayesian hierarchical framework with an adapted N-mixture model to pool information across sites and estimate total fatalities for ten bat species across the conterminous United States from 1981 to 2024. Our analysis predicts approximately 18.7 million bat fatalities over this period, with substantially higher species-specific totals than previously estimated. Our framework provides a landscape-level analysis that can predict fatalities for unmonitored locations and years, identify landscape-level drivers of fatalities, produce a multidecade hindcast of cumulative losses due to wind energy, and map where species-specific risk is highest. Although limitations and uncertainty remain, the magnitude of predicted fatalities may be comparable to total losses from white-nose syndrome, another major threat to North American bat populations. These threats affect largely different species, suggesting their impacts may compound, but updated population-level impact assessments could reveal potential cumulative effects. Our estimates of species-specific covariate relationships with rotor-swept area, ground clearance, land cover, and proximity to rivers, highlight opportunities to help reduce impacts through wind turbine design and siting. This work establishes a generalizable landscape-level framework for evaluating wildlife fatalities at wind energy facilities and highlights how coordinated monitoring, data sharing, and population-level impact assessments could further inform conservation efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Regulation of miR-219 and its target RalGPS is essential for synaptic plasticity at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction
articles_hidden.authors: Kumar Aavula, Hansine Heggeness, Takakazu Yokokura, Spyros Artavanis-Tsakonas, David Van Vactor
articles_hidden.abstract: RNA regulatory mechanisms mediate adaptive responses relying on rapid changes in gene expression. By examining microRNA (miRNA)-mediated control of structural synaptic plasticity, we find miR-219 and five other conserved miRNAs regulate activity-induced morphogenesis at Drosophila glutamatergic synapses. Among miRNA targets downregulated by acute stimulation, the Ral activating factor RalGPS is necessary for presynaptic morphogenesis and is sufficient to block plasticity. We find that RalGPS must be held within a narrow range of expression for structural remodeling to occur. Loss or excess of RalGPS both abolish activity-induced synapse growth. Without altering levels of mature miR-219, stimulation elevates miR-219 loading in Argonaute (Ago1)-containing complexes that mediate miRNA gene silencing. We also find that elevated Protein Kinase A activity suppresses miR-219 association with Ago1 and blocks activity-induced synaptic growth, suggesting that miRNA loading and unloading in neurons are both controlled by activity-dependent regulation of Ago1.

articles_hidden.title: Pancreatic δ cells are resistant to auto- and paracrine inhibition in human type-2 diabetes
articles_hidden.authors: Muhmmad Omar-Hmeadi, Lina Matuseviciene, Liangwen Liu, Per-Eric Lund, Sebastian Barg
articles_hidden.abstract: Somatostatin secretion from pancreatic δ cells inhibits nearby α- and β cells and tunes the body’s glycemic set-point. The role of δ cells in diabetes remains unclear, in part due to the difficulty separating intrinsic regulation from intraislet paracrine effects. Here, we compared the function of isolated δ cells of cadaveric nondiabetic and type-2 diabetic donors by single cell total internal reflection microscopy, electrophysiology, and secretion measurements. Elevated glucose stimulated exocytosis of somatostatin, which was further amplified by glucagon, exendin-4, or forskolin, independent of diabetic status. gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) enhanced exocytosis and electrical activity, while insulin had no detectable effect. Adrenaline and somatostatin strongly inhibited δ cell activity, leading to autocrine feedback inhibition of somatostatin exocytosis. In type-2 diabetes, δ cell inhibition by somatostatin and adrenaline was impaired, together with a marked reduction in somatostatin receptor (SSTR2) surface expression. The data suggest that selective loss of inhibitory control of δ cells may dysregulate intraislet somatostatin signaling in type-2 diabetes.

articles_hidden.title: Holocene millennial climate variability influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Peng Zhou, Zhengguo Shi, Zhisheng An, Wenju Cai, Pascale Braconnot, Qiong Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: A prominent unstable feature, millennial-scale climate oscillation (MCO), punctuated the Holocene. Solar activity and deep ocean variability are generally regarded as the origin of the MCO, yet the dynamics remain debated. Using a Holocene transient simulation with the EC-Earth climate model (8 to 0 ka BP), together with a global compilation of 304 temperature reconstructions, here we identify a robust ~1,350-y oscillatory mode that characterizes Holocene climate variability and is self-sustained and crucially influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions. Within each cycle, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) strengthening evolves with the developing warming and an El Niño-like tropical sea surface temperature (SST) response, accompanied by anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Northward cold advection of the associated enhanced westerly winds off the Antarctic coast overcomes the effect of sea ice retreat to promote AABW formation, ocean stratification, and warming. Positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo, tropical air–sea interaction, and SST-AABW magnify surface warming till AABW reaches its peak. Thereafter, reduced brine rejection from sea-ice retreat weakens AABW, counteracts the warming, and commences a switch to its cooling phase. The dominant periodicity, consistent with that inferred from proxy reconstructions, is confirmed by complementary climate simulations. These results provide an alternative physical mechanism for Holocene millennial-scale climate variability. Under future anthropogenic warming, a positive phase of the oscillation may heighten the positive feedbacks, thereby increasing the risk of rapid climate transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Annexins cooperate with Myomaker to promote myoblast fusion
articles_hidden.authors: Zhisheng Xu, Key Tse, Ning Liu, Eric N. Olson
articles_hidden.abstract: Myoblast fusion is essential for skeletal muscle development and regeneration. Myomaker is a muscle-specific fusogen indispensable for this process. Cryoelectron microscopy analysis has shown that Myomaker dimerization is required for myoblast fusion and muscle formation. However, the precise molecular mechanisms of Myomaker function remain unclear. Notably, the short extracellular domain of Myomaker suggests the involvement of additional proteins that cooperate with Myomaker to facilitate membrane fusion. To identify potential interacting partners of Myomaker, we employed an APEX2-based proximity labeling approach in a synchronized myoblast fusion and differentiation system. By comparing results with a fusion-deficient mutant form of Myomaker, we identified several members of the Annexin family of calcium-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins as prominent candidates for interaction, particularly under prefusion conditions. Among these, Annexins A2, A5, and A6 were found to colocalize with Myomaker at the myoblast plasma membrane. Proximity ligation assays further confirmed the close association of these Annexins with Myomaker at the cell surface. Functional analyses demonstrated that these Annexins can promote heterologous cell–cell fusion between fibroblasts and myoblasts. While single knockdown of Annexin A2, A5, or A6 had minimal effects, the simultaneous knockdown of all three impaired myoblast fusion, indicating functional redundancy among them. Together, these findings indicate that Annexins A2, A5, and A6 cooperate with Myomaker to promote myoblast fusion, providing a mechanistic link between the fusogenic machinery and membrane dynamics during myoblast fusion.

articles_hidden.title: Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Beccaria, Abraham Muñiz-Chicharro, Rebecca C. Wade
articles_hidden.abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

articles_hidden.title: Restructuring the nitrogen cycle and sparing cropland by feeding insect-derived protein to global livestock
articles_hidden.authors: Jerome Dumortier

articles_hidden.title: In vitro binding energies capture Klf4 occupancy across the human genome
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Schwager, Jonas Neipel, Yahor Savich, Douglas Diehl, Frank Jülicher, Anthony A. Hyman, Stephan W. Grill
articles_hidden.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) regulate gene expression by binding to specific genomic loci determined by DNA sequence. Their sequence specificity is commonly summarized by a consensus binding motif. However, eukaryotic genomes contain billions of low-affinity DNA sequences to which TFs associate with a sequence-dependent binding energy. We currently lack insight into how the genomic sequence defines this spectrum of binding energies and the resulting pattern of TF localization. Here, we set out to obtain a quantitative understanding of sequence-dependent TF binding to both motif and nonmotif sequences. We achieve this by first pursuing accurate measurements of physical binding energies of human TF Krüppel-like factor 4 (Klf4) to a library of short DNA sequences in a fluorescence-anisotropy-based bulk competitive binding assay. Second, we show that the highly nonlinear sequence dependence of Klf4 binding energies can be captured by combining a linear model of binding energies with an Ising model of the coupled recognition of nucleotides by a TF. In this model, nucleotide–TF interfaces collectively switch between two states, weak binding and strong nucleotide-specific binding, and the states of neighboring interfaces are coupled with J ∼ 2 k B T . We find that this statistical mechanics model parameterized by our in vitro measurements captures Klf4 binding patterns on an individual long DNA molecule stretched in the optical tweezer, and is predictive for Klf4 occupancy across the entire human genome without additional fit parameters.

articles_hidden.title: New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Berger, Amira Naimi, Kornelia Hardes, Claudia Sachße, Ricarda Gericke, Michael Marner, Felix Mühlemeyer, Tanja Pommerening, Raphael Reher
articles_hidden.abstract: Mumia vera aegyptiaca was a mummy-derived medicinal substance widely used in medieval and early modern medicine, yet its material composition and biological activity remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate Egyptological and pharmaceutical-historical analysis of 41 textual sources with LC–MS/MS-based metabolomics, molecular networking, machine-learning-assisted annotation, and bioactivity testing to investigate ancient Egyptian embalming materials and historical Mumia vera samples. We analyzed 24 objects from university and pharmacy museum collections, including historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. Comparative metabolomics revealed substantial heterogeneity among materials labeled as Mumia vera , but also recurrent molecular signatures consistent with aged conifer resins, including oxidized abietane-type diterpenoids. Several samples contained Aloe -associated metabolites, including aloeresin A/D- and aloin-related compounds. These data reveal Aloe -associated metabolites in ancient Egyptian embalming-related materials and support the presence of Aloe spp.-derived exudates in selected samples. The convergence of molecular and textual evidence further raises the possibility that a previously unresolved Egyptian term from the 2nd millennium BC may refer to Aloe sp. or an Aloe -derived product. Comparative metabolomics also linked an inconspicuous powder sample to a specific mummified head, although their curatorial association had not been securely documented. Finally, a historical Mumia vera aegyptiaca extract modestly protected MDCK cells from influenza virus-induced cytopathic effects, whereas the isolated major compound 7-oxodehydroabietic acid was inactive on its own. Together, these findings show how integrating textual scholarship, pharmaceutical history, and molecular analysis can refine the interpretation of ancient Egyptian embalming practices, museum objects, and historical medicines.

articles_hidden.title: Intraventricular clindamycin enhances interstitial brain fluid drainage and the blood–brain barrier after a traumatic brain injury
articles_hidden.authors: Landon S. Ashby, Megan G. Crowe, Daveraj Chakravarty, Sanjeev Medam, Gabriel Frampton, Ayesha B. Das, David A. Hormuth, Thomas E. Yankeelov, Vincent Y. C. Wang, Linda J. Noble-Haeusslein, Benjamin J. Umlauf
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite advances in the acute clinical management of severe traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), treating injury-derived secondary pathogenesis remains challenging. We demonstrate intracerebroventricular (I.C.V.) administration of clindamycin alleviates TBI secondary pathogenesis in both focal and diffuse murine models of brain injury. I.C.V. administration of clindamycin increased the motility of ependymal cilia, which line the ventricles and spinal canal, by 30 to 60%, which correlated with interstitial brain fluid drainage through the cortex (r > 0.9 Pearson, n = 4 compounds tested). I.C.V. clindamycin treatment post-TBI also restored the blood–brain barrier (BBB), decreased lesion size, and lowered serum levels of glial fibrillary acidic protein by 2.8-fold. Consistent with these data, a novel objective recognition test revealed an improvement in recognition memory in brain-injured mice treated with clindamycin. These collective findings reveal a counterintuitive finding that I.C.V. clindamycin enhances drainage of toxins from the brain while simultaneously restoring the BBB, potentially providing a new solution for alleviating secondary pathogenesis in brain-injured patients.

articles_hidden.title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons
articles_hidden.authors: Huanxin Zhang, Weizhi Huang, Shihao Xu, Guy M. Genin, Xiangjun Peng, Xi-Qiao Feng
articles_hidden.abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

articles_hidden.title: The efficiency of information gain by natural selection
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan Seamus McGee, Olivia Kosterlitz, Artem Kaznatcheev, Benjamin Kerr, Carl T. Bergstrom
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural selection enriches populations for genotypes that are well adapted to their environments, accumulating information about the selective conditions in the process. Therefore, selection can be viewed as a learning process through which populations acquire information about the environment. Motoo Kimura derived a relationship between the amount of information gained by selection and a measure of the inefficiency of the selective process, known as substitution load [M. Kimura, Genet. Res. 2, 127–140 (1961)]. Due to the gradual nature of selection and the ongoing mismatch of types to the environment, a lineage that is still acquiring information has lower mean fitness than a lineage that already has it. While this has been an influential insight, we find that Kimura’s model is inconsistent with selection experiments involving Escherichia coli . To address limitations in this model and develop a more robust measure for the efficiency of selection, we turn to computational learning theory. We show that the learning-theoretic concept of regret quantifies the inefficiency of selection as a learning process in terms of relative lineage fitness. We establish bounds on the efficiency of information gain in general settings, including frequency-dependent selection and arbitrary environmental change. We experimentally validate these bounds and demonstrate that our extended theory recovers Kimura’s fundamental insight. Finally, we show that selection is an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the basic problem faced by evolving populations and that it acquires information more efficiently than comparable processes in complex environments.

articles_hidden.title: Cooperative nature of residue interactions in biomolecular condensates
articles_hidden.authors: Le Chen, Xiangyu Wu, Guorong Hu, Xiangze Zeng, Jingyuan Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Cooperativity of residue interactions is prevalent in proteins and plays an essential role in protein folding. However, whether cooperativity exists in intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their assembled biomolecular condensates remains elusive. Here, we reveal the presence of residue interaction cooperativity in various IDP condensates using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. In all these condensates, cooperative residue interactions manifest as packing between finite residue motifs (3 to 5 residues) with lifetimes three orders of magnitude longer than residue contacts. Notably, these higher-order interactions (HOIs) exhibit a significant nonadditive free energy, which originates from a local low-dielectric environment. The underlying sequence patterns like “Y-X-Q”, “D-X-R”, and “S-Y-X” are identified. Furthermore, HOIs dominate the cohesive energy of IDPs and condensates can be treated as HOI-crosslinked networks. This model can successfully reproduce experimental results of condensate physical properties, including saturation concentration, viscoelasticity, and interfacial tension.

articles_hidden.title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor–regulated endothelial PD-L1
articles_hidden.authors: Yiu Ming Cheung, Hoi Wa Yeung, Chufeng He, Qile Zhang, Chui Yiu Bamboo Chook, Gary Tse, Yun Liao, Wing Tak Wong
articles_hidden.abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.

articles_hidden.title: Anchoring Anatolian tree-rings and Mesopotamian chronology with single-year radiocarbon patterns and ice-core evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Pearson, Nicolas Brehm, Lukas Wacker, Peter Brewer, Michael Sigl, Peter Kuniholm, Kurt Nicolussi, Matthew Salzer, Alex Bayliss
articles_hidden.abstract: The historical chronology of Mesopotamia offers a key chronological bridge to connect the Near East and eastern Mediterranean during the second millennium BCE. It is unusually rich in written records, including king lists, administrative documents, royal inscriptions, and astronomical observations. The latter offer a number of alternate possible absolute anchor points, resulting in competing high, middle, low, and ultra-low temporal frameworks. Establishing which of these is correct has consequences far beyond Mesopotamia. Tree-ring sequences from preserved timbers at archaeological sites in Anatolia, linked directly to Mesopotamia via the Old Assyrian trade network, could provide the answer. However, attempts have been limited by the lack of calendar secured dendrochronological dating for these timbers. Here we develop transferable methodologies in single-year radiocarbon analysis, utilizing patterns of 14 C preserved in single tree rings from Anatolian timbers to anchor their combined chronology 2072 BCE–744 BCE. This provides a calendrically-secured reference chronology for wood samples from Anatolian sites during this period as well as an annually resolved paleoclimatic record. Tree-ring dates are combined with archaeological and high-resolution ice-core evidence to evaluate the competing chronological frameworks for Mesopotamia between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Remaining dating uncertainties are constrained in strong support of the middle–low chronology.

articles_hidden.title: Encoding metal coordination pathways and nuclearity by molecular knotting
articles_hidden.authors: Guanyu Chi, Bo Li, Hai-Na Feng, Zhi-Hui Zhang, Heng Wang, Xiaopeng Li, Liang Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Precise control over the nuclearity and spatial organization of metal ions is a central objective in coordination chemistry. Knotting imposes severe geometric constraints on frameworks but has rarely been exploited to organize inequivalent metal-binding sites within a single ligand. Here we report that a molecular cinquefoil knot containing both bidentate and tridentate chelating sites enables programmed metal-ion coordination pathways. Direct metalation affords Mn(II) 5 -, Fe(II) 5 -, Co(II) 5 -, and Cd(II) 5 -knots through a dinuclear intermediate and an unusual 2-to-5 metal nuclearity progression, even though these metals do not template knot formation. Crystallization of a Mn(II) 2 -intermediate reveals partial demetalation but retains a Mn(II) center displaying a “3 + 3” coordination mode, whereas all Fe(II) ions in the fully metalated Fe(II) 5 -knot adopt a “3 + 2” binding geometry. Together with computational simulations, these observations support a stepwise metalation mechanism in which the dinuclear “3 + 3” coordination environment evolves into the “3 + 2” motif of the pentanuclear knot. Although the Ni(II) 5 - knot cannot be obtained by direct metalation because of slow incorporation, it forms readily via transmetalation from a Zn(II) 5 -knot. Circular dichroism measurements show that chiral expression is dictated by the overall ligand arrangement rather than the identity of the metal ions. The work demonstrates molecular knotting as a strategy for pathway-controlled multi-metallic assembly.

articles_hidden.title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
articles_hidden.authors: Jasmine A. Therrien, Terry Huebert, Preetam Janakirama, Emine Kaplanoglu, Lavinia I. Fechete, Susanne Kohalmi, Stig U. Andersen, Jens Stougaard, Loretta Ross, Krzysztof Szczyglowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.

articles_hidden.title: Reply to Zhou and Tsao: Synergy rarely underlies the benefits of combination cancer therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Nicole A. Traphagen Ho, Myles Brown

articles_hidden.title: circEPSTI1 regulates miR-942-5p–SERPINE1–AKT1 signaling axis to enhance dengue infection and is suppressed by Tiplaxtinin
articles_hidden.authors: Nilanjana Das, Pandikannan Krishnamoorthy, Kushal Ramrao Junghare, Athira S. Raj, Priyanka Saha, Kuhu Pal, Shouvanik Adhya, Atul Garg, Dheeraj Khetan, Ashok Kumar, Himanshu Kumar
articles_hidden.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have recently been identified as crucial regulators of gene expression in various diseases. Their role in dengue remains unexplored. In this study, circEPSTI1 induction was observed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and plasma of dengue patients. The induction of circEPSTI1 is interferon-dependent and enhances DENV infection by sponging the expression of miR-942-5p. The antiviral role of miR-942-5p is mediated by bidirectional inhibition through targeting conserved genomic sequences of the DENV genome of different subtypes across NS1, NS3, and NS5 and the host AKT1 signaling pathway. RNA-seq analysis of DENV-infected circEPSTI1 knockdown A549 cells identified SERPINE1 and AKT1 signaling pathways to be dysregulated significantly. circEPSTI1 relieves the inhibition of miR-942-5p over DENV genomic RNA and the host SERPINE1 to activate AKT1 signaling. The activation of AKT1 signaling facilitates cell survival and enhances DENV replication. The expression of SERPINE1 and circEPSTI1 was upregulated in Dengue patients, and pharmaceutical inhibition of SERPINE1 through Tiplaxtinin inhibits the DENV replication by reducing the expression of circEPSTI1. Overall, our result demonstrates the therapeutic potential of Tiplaxtinin by targeting the circEPSTI1–miR-942-5p–SERPINE1–AKT1 axis in dengue treatment.
